title: Overshoot, Paper, Descenders, Two Numbers & a Withdrawn Declaration
description: Unclamped progress(), @page margin boxes, underlines that clear descenders, spring motion as CSS properties, and revert-rule.

drops.title: Overshoot From One Number
drops.description: One driver value walks 0 to 1; four lanes map it through their own windows, and one is free to run past the ends.
drops.concept: CSS progress() turns a single driver value into as many curves as you need — each lane declares its own from/to window and gets back a number the browser interpolates. Safari 27 added the no-clamp option, which lets the result escape 0–1 so motion can anticipate and overshoot without a keyframe in sight. The page falls back to the same arithmetic in script where progress() isn't available yet.

interaction.mouse: Drag the scrub slider to walk the driver by hand
interaction.click: Pause, play and toggle ping-pong; widen or narrow the overshoot window
interaction.touch: All controls are sliders and buttons — the panel becomes a block on narrow screens

drops.title: Sixteen Boxes Around the Type
drops.description: @page gives a sheet its margins, sixteen margin boxes and two counters — a layout system browsers shipped and few use.
drops.concept: A printed page is not a scrolling box. @page sets the sheet size and margins, and the margin area is divided into sixteen addressable boxes that take running heads, folios and counter(page) of counter(pages). Chrome has supported margin boxes since 131 and Safari since 18.2. Three on-screen proofs share their geometry with the live @page rule through custom properties, so dragging a margin moves the screen and the paper together.
drops.source: Doppio — CSS Page Margin Boxes & Page Numbers

interaction.mouse: Drag the margin sliders and watch the page area give and take
interaction.click: Switch sheet size, toggle the guides and columns, or open the print preview
interaction.touch: Sheets scale down and the panel moves inline

drops.title: Underlines That Clear the Descenders
drops.description: skip-ink cuts holes in the line; text-underline-position moves the whole line out of the way instead.
drops.concept: Every underline has to decide what to do about a j, a g or a Vietnamese tone mark. text-decoration-skip-ink breaks the line around them, which works for Latin and falls apart for scripts that hang a long way below the baseline. text-underline-position: under drops the line below the content box entirely, and in vertical writing modes the same property picks a side. The W3C's i18n guide is candid that results still depend on the font — so the demo gives you offset, thickness and a magnifier to check.

interaction.mouse: Slide type size, offset, thickness and the inspect zoom
interaction.click: Toggle skip-ink and cycle Latin / Vietnamese / mixed specimens
interaction.touch: Specimens stack and the panel moves inline

drops.title: Motion as a CSS Property
drops.description: One spring loop writes --k-x and --k-y; every tilt, glare, depth and parallax layer is a plain CSS declaration.
drops.concept: Kinesis.js makes the point that interactive motion can be configuration rather than code: the library springs a handful of custom properties and leaves the composition to CSS. This reimplementation keeps the shape of that idea — a damped spring per region writes two registered numbers, and tilt, counter-rotation, depth offset, magnetic pull and three parallax layers all read them. Effects use translate and rotate rather than transform, so an author's own transforms survive.

interaction.mouse: Move the pointer over any panel — tilt, glare and parallax follow on a spring
interaction.click: Pick a spring preset, or drag stiffness, damping, tilt and depth
interaction.touch: Without hover the regions drift on a slow orbit so the effect still reads

drops.title: A Declaration That Can Withdraw
drops.description: Three identical components, three attr() fallbacks — only revert-rule hands the decision back to the rule underneath.
drops.concept: revert-rule rolls a property back to the value it would have had without the current style rule — narrower than revert-layer, which drops the whole cascade layer. Its sharpest use is as an attr() fallback: when the attribute isn't there the declaration simply bows out, instead of forcing a guessed value. Here the same component is styled three ways; pull the attributes off and one guesses, one loses the theme default with the layer, and one lands exactly where it should.

interaction.mouse: Drag radius and padding to feed the attributes the rule reads
interaction.click: Toggle the attributes off and compare the three fallbacks side by side
interaction.touch: Cards stack on narrow screens; the panel moves inline
